Beijing should honor deal on Korean films and games A day ahead of the historic trilateral meeting between China, the U.S. and Russia, President Lee Jae Myung lifted a hurdle for Korean cultural content in a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, Wednesday. A decade into an unofficial ban China has not formally acknowledged, the two leaders' agreement is expected to clear a path for Korean cultural products.
Lee and Xi met for 34 minutes on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, follow-up second-phase free trade negotiations on services and investment that began in 2018. The agreement includes Beijing granting Seoul the most-favored nation status for its movies and games, allowing Korean travel agencies to advance into China's 23 regions and Korean companies to independently operate their brand shops in China as well. China also agreed to apply nondiscrimination principles to the review of online games, films and other content, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources.
The agreement is fueling anticipation that more Korean content will freely access the Chinese market, including K-pop, which has largely been excluded since China protested Korea's decision to deploy a U.S. Terminal High Altitude Area Defense anti-missile defense system in 2016. Since then, Korean content faced an unofficial barrier, including the cancellation of scheduled K-pop performances. In order not to spoil the anticipation, specific tasks remain ahead, and they should be aligned with the spirit expressed by Lee and Xi during their meeting in Shenzhen.
Just as Lee underscored the importance of peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula, the president noted that Korea-China relations are on the "road to solid recovery," and that he wanted "the strategic cooperative partnership between Korea and China to develop in a mature manner." In response, Xi described Korea and China as "close, friendly neighbors and strategic cooperative partners" with a common goal of "improving the lives of our people."
Many issues are intertwined between the two nations, both direct and pivotal for the affairs on the Korean Peninsula. But the exchange of popular content, by nature, can enable fluid cultural and commercial exchanges. There is more room for Korean services exports to China to grow. According to 2024 trade figures, trade in goods with China stood at 20.7 percent of Korea's total goods trade, while services trade accounted for 12.4 percent. The Korean trade ministry estimated that the bilateral trade between the two nations in services and investment is currently around $38.3 billion. Lee pointed out that Chinese travelers to Korea are expected to reach 10 million this year for the first time since 2019.
Until Korea and China cement the trade agreement, the expectation for that figure invariably will be upward. On Thursday, the stock prices for Korea's top entertainment agencies, including HYBE, SM Entertainment and JYP Entertainment, rose for the second day.
The optimism however is juxtaposed with a realistic outlook that the trade agreement does not mention large-scale K-pop performances in China. Various Korean experts have said that whether those performances will be allowed may well be the litmus test of further cultural exchanges. As is the case, the Korean government must continue to discuss, persuade and negotiate with China to enable such exchanges. Beijing should also play a part by formalizing and implementing the agreement and ensuring that the exchanges are carried out on the regional level as well.
As international relations cannot eschew reciprocity, Seoul should prepare for possible demands from Beijing. The Chinese president also expressed the need for the two nations to "foster a cooperative ecosystem for emerging technology industries such as artificial intelligence." Korea, which upholds an alliance as well as a trade partnership with the U.S., should manage potentially differing interests through robust dialogue and communications with its invaluable partner nations.
